story.title: Lindsay Clancy Trial Jury Continues Deliberations Amid Mistrial Concerns
story.summary: The jury in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial has returned for a sixth day of deliberations after previously reporting deadlock. The jurors have expressed difficulty in reaching a unanimous verdict, raising the possibility of a mistrial as Judge William Sullivan oversees the proceedings. The trial has garnered significant public attention since it began six weeks ago.

event_overview.title: About Lindsay Clancy Trial
event_overview.subject: Lindsay Clancy Trial
event_overview.summary: The Lindsay Clancy trial is a Massachusetts criminal proceeding over the deaths of Clancy’s three children at the family’s home in Duxbury in January 2023. The central legal question is whether the prosecution can prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the alleged killings, after she raised lack of criminal responsibility in connection with postpartum mental illness.

facts.label: Underlying incident
facts.value: Authorities say Duxbury police responded on January 24, 2023, and found three children—Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy—who later died; the deaths were investigated by Duxbury Police and the Massachusetts State Police Detective Unit assigned to the Plymouth County District Attorney’s Office.

facts.label: Charges and pleas
facts.value: A Plymouth County grand jury indicted Clancy on September 15, 2023, on three murder counts and three strangulation counts. At her October 26, 2023 Superior Court arraignment, she pleaded not guilty; ahead of trial, prosecutors dropped the three strangulation charges, leaving three murder counts for trial.

facts.label: Court and trial status
facts.value: The case is being tried in Plymouth County Superior Court in Massachusetts. As of August 31, 2026, a jury was deliberating after a five-week trial.

facts.label: Legal standard at issue
facts.value: Under Massachusetts’s lack-of-criminal-responsibility standard, once the issue is raised, the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant did not lack substantial capacity, because of mental disease or defect, either to appreciate the wrongfulness or criminality of the conduct or to conform conduct to the law.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows late-July through August 31, 2026 trial developments, especially the competing postpartum-psychosis evidence, mistrial request and jury deliberations; it does not attempt to reproduce the full investigation, pretrial record or all testimony.

explore_lenses.label: Why is the jury deadlocked?
explore_lenses.title: The dispute is over criminal responsibility
explore_lenses.summary: Clancy’s lawyers do not dispute that she killed her children; the central question is whether mental illness left her legally not criminally responsible at that time. The sharply opposed psychiatric evidence and competing accounts of planning versus psychosis make unanimity difficult.

claims.text: Jurors are weighing five possible outcomes: first- or second-degree murder, manslaughter, not guilty, or not guilty by reason of insanity.
Defense attorney Kevin Reddington argues that Clancy was overmedicated and experiencing postpartum psychosis, so she was not criminally responsible.
Prosecutors contend that Clancy planned the killings and understood that her actions were wrong; prosecution and defense psychiatric experts reached different conclusions about her mental state.

explore_lenses.label: Why does the second deadlock matter?
explore_lenses.title: The case is at a late procedural stage
explore_lenses.summary: The second impasse prompted Judge William Sullivan to give the Massachusetts Tuey-Rodriguez instruction, which urges conscientious further deliberation while guarding against coercion. Massachusetts model instructions place special limits on sending a jury back out after it returns a second time without a verdict.

claims.text: By September 3, the jury had deliberated for more than 30 hours over six days and had twice reported that it could not reach a unanimous verdict.
Judge Sullivan gave a Tuey-Rodriguez, or “dynamite,” instruction after the second deadlock, telling jurors to continue their effort to reach a verdict.

Massachusetts’ model instruction says that after a jury returns a second time without agreeing, it generally may not be sent out again without its consent, except when it seeks further legal explanation.

explore_lenses.label: What would a mistrial change?
explore_lenses.title: It would end this trial, not necessarily the case
explore_lenses.summary: A mistrial based on a hung jury would leave no verdict on the charges and would not itself resolve Clancy’s criminal responsibility. The next decision would shift to prosecutors, while both sides could use information from jurors’ post-trial views to reassess strategy.

claims.text: If a mistrial is declared because the jury cannot agree, prosecutors may retry the case, pursue different charges, seek a plea agreement, or drop charges, according to legal experts cited by ABC News.

Reddington said he would be ready for a second trial “next week,” while CBS legal contributor Caroline Polisi said lawyers would likely seek jurors’ views because those views could shape any retrial strategy.
Forecast: Polisi said she thought a verdict was unlikely and that another report of hopeless deadlock would most likely require a mistrial to avoid pressuring jurors into a coercive verdict.

story_report.summary: Jurors in Lindsay Clancy’s trial over the January 2023 deaths of her three children resumed deliberations after more than 30 hours across six days and two reports that they could not reach a unanimous verdict. Judge William Sullivan instructed them to continue trying to agree, but a mistrial remains possible if the panel cannot do so. No mistrial had been declared as of Sept. 3, 2026.

sections.heading: Clancy Mental-State Defense and Prosecution Case
sections.body: Jurors are weighing first- or second-degree murder, manslaughter, not guilty, or not guilty by reason of insanity. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington argues that Clancy was overmedicated and experiencing postpartum psychosis, leaving her not criminally responsible. Prosecutors contend she planned the killings and knew her actions were wrong; psychiatric experts for the two sides reached differing conclusions about her mental state.

sections.heading: Massachusetts Rules on Deadlocked Juries
sections.body: Sullivan gave the jury a Tuey-Rodriguez instruction, sometimes called a “dynamite” instruction, after its second deadlock report. Under Massachusetts’ model instruction, a jury that returns a second time without agreement generally cannot be sent back to deliberate without its consent, except when it requests additional legal explanation. A finding that the panel is hopelessly deadlocked could result in a mistrial.

sections.heading: Potential Consequences of a Mistrial
sections.body: If a mistrial is declared because jurors cannot agree, prosecutors could retry the case, seek different charges, pursue a plea agreement or drop the charges, according to legal experts cited by ABC News. Reddington said he would be ready for another trial “next week.” CBS legal contributor Caroline Polisi said lawyers would likely seek jurors’ views, which could affect strategy in any retrial.

The Plymouth County District Attorney had not publicly said whether the case would be retried if a mistrial were declared.
